re-correlophus-ciliatus.title: Crested Gecko
re-correlophus-ciliatus.summary: A tree-climbing gecko from New Caledonia that eats mostly a prepared fruit-based diet. ReptiFiles rates it low difficulty.
rows: About 8 in snout to tail. Adults weigh 35–45 g
Tall, climbing setup: 18 × 18 × 36 in (L × W × H) minimum for one adult
Top (warm) 82–85°F, bottom 70–75°F, night 65–72°F. Avoid long stretches above 85°F
60–80%. Mist daily, and let it dry to about 50% between mistings to prevent mold
Low-level UVB is recommended (UVI 1–2 at the top branch). Day/night cycle, no night lights
Complete powdered crested gecko diet mixed with water. Juveniles get it daily plus insects 1–2× a week. Adults get it every 2–3 days plus insects 0–1× a week. Fruit only as an occasional treat
Build up slowly. Start with 5-minute sessions every other day, then go up to about 15 minutes once it stays calm (no more than about 20 minutes a day). They jump, so handle over a soft surface
Most active at dusk and dawn. Climbs and leaps
notes: A dropped tail does not grow back.
Don't house males together. Two females need at least twice the minimum space.

re-hemitheconyx-caudicinctus.title: African Fat-Tailed Gecko
re-hemitheconyx-caudicinctus.summary: A docile, ground-dwelling gecko from West African savanna, closely related to the leopard gecko. It has eyelids, can't climb glass, stores fat in its plump tail, and is usually easy to handle.
rows: 36 × 18 × 18 in (L × W × H) minimum for one; they can climb rocks, so add some low climbing
Warm hide 90–94°F, cool side 72–77°F, night 72–77°F (a cooler, drier winter period is used for breeding)
Warm/rainy season about 70–80% by day and up to 100% at night; dry season about 50% by day. Always provide a humid hide on the cool end
Can survive without UVB if given a D3 calcium supplement, but low-level UVB is recommended. Lights off at night
Insectivore. Feed a variety of insects lightly dusted with calcium, with a multivitamin now and then
Usually very docile and tolerant of handling
Nocturnal; hides by day in dark, humid spots
West Africa, Senegal to Nigeria and northern Cameroon (Sahel and savanna)
notes: Best kept one per enclosure; males in particular fight.

sources.name: ReptiFiles – African Fat-Tailed Gecko Care Sheet

re-coleonyx-mitratus.title: Central American Banded Gecko
re-coleonyx-mitratus.summary: A slim, banded eyelid gecko from Guatemala to Costa Rica. It hides in burrows by day and comes out at dusk to hunt insects. Hardy and small, it suits a modest terrarium with a humid hide.
rows: About 4–5 in (up to 190 mm including the tail, about half of which is tail)
A 10-gal tank can hold two or three adults; give several hides and a mostly dry substrate (e.g. coco fiber) with one moist area
Ambient 75–80°F with a daytime hot spot of about 90–92°F (heat pad or lamp)
50–60%, plus a humid hide (e.g. damp sphagnum). Mist 4–5× a week; it should dry within a few hours
Insects only: dubia roaches or crickets as staples, small mealworms or waxworms as treats. Insects no longer than the space between the eyes; dust with supplements
Crepuscular (dawn and dusk); hides underground by day
Central America, Guatemala to Costa Rica (semi-arid areas to humid forest)
notes: Males are aggressive to each other; don't house males together.
Can drop its tail if threatened; it usually regrows within a year.

sources.name: Josh's Frogs – Central American banded gecko care

re-lygodactylus-luteopicturatus.title: Yellow-Headed Dwarf Gecko
re-lygodactylus-luteopicturatus.summary: A tiny, fast, day-active gecko from coastal East Africa. Males have a bright yellow head and blue-gray body; females are duller. It climbs smooth surfaces, eats small insects plus nectar and soft fruit, and needs UVB and warm basking.
rows: About 7–9 cm (3–3.5 in) including the tail
Planted climbing setup with many branches and a climbable back wall (e.g. cork); pine bark or soil substrate with leaf litter and cork hides
Day 77–90°F (25–32°C) with a local basking spot; night 64–72°F (18–22°C)
UV lighting required: a T5 fluorescent tube plus a local basking lamp
Small insects (crickets, flies, small roaches) plus overripe banana, unsweetened fruit mash or nectar offered regularly; use vitamin supplements
Active by day; an agile climber
Southern Kenya, eastern Tanzania and Zanzibar (rocky areas, woods, plantations)
notes: Keep as a pair or one male with 2–3 females; never more than one male.
Some authors treat it as part of L. picturatus.
